title: 03 - Justice

content.text: Syllabus — Justice: conceptions of justice with special reference to Rawls’ theory of justice and its communitarian critique. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 3)

justice as an architectonic and dynamic idea; classical (Plato, Aristotle) and modern theories; the types/dimensions of justice (distributive, procedural vs substantive, retributive); Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’; and its critiques — Nozick (libertarian), Amartya Sen (methodological) and the communitarians (Sandel, Walzer, Taylor, MacIntyre), with Rawls’ reply in Political Liberalism.

Plato, Aristotle, Hume, David Miller, John Rawls, Robert Nozick, Amartya Sen, Ronald Dworkin, Michael Sandel, Michael Walzer, Charles Taylor, Alasdair MacIntyre, Carole Gilligan, Thomas Pogge, A.V. Dicey.

Rawls dominates — original position (2013), difference principle (2015), contractual & distributive (2017), justification of discrimination (2018), Rawls enriching liberalism (2021); plus Greek vs Rawlsian (2020), communitarian perspectives (2019) and distributive justice (2018).

Q — Explain Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’ — the original position, veil of ignorance, primary goods, maximin, the two principles and lexical order, the difference principle and democratic equality. Is it both contractual and distributive? (UPSC 2013/2015/2017/2018/2021)
Lay out Rawls’ machinery step by step, then prove it is at once a social contract and a scheme of redistribution.
: no person may be sacrificed for the aggregate.
(Utilitarianism could justify displacing a tribal village for a dam because more people gain; Rawls forbids it.)
— a hypothetical ‘thought experiment’ in which rational, mutually disinterested people frame the rules before society exists.
(Like drafting the Constitution before knowing which caste, class or religion you will be born into.)
— stripped of knowledge of class, caste, sex and talent, risk-averse agents pick the option whose
(Not knowing whether you will be born a Delhi industrialist or a landless Dalit, you insure the bottom rung.)
— (1) equal basic liberty; (2) fair equality of opportunity + the difference principle.
= principle 1 must be fully satisfied before 2 is even considered.
(No amount of poverty relief may buy away the right to vote or to free speech.)
— inequality is legitimate only if it lifts the
(A surgeon may earn ten times a clerk if the higher pay is what staffs rural PHCs; reservation is defended on the same logic.)
— a hypothetical agreement (Locke, Rousseau, Kant) that also redistributes
, whom the text calls “the greatest political philosopher of the 20th century,” revived normative theory in
with ‘justice as fairness’. He writes against

, which permits the individual to be sacrificed for the ‘greatest happiness of the greatest number’ — as when a tribal village is displaced for a dam because the aggregate gain is larger. Reviving the
tradition of human dignity, his theory is
: “each person possesses an inviolability founded on justice that even the welfare of society as a whole cannot override.”

is a hypothetical, purely procedural ‘thought experiment’ — not a historical state of nature — in which rational, mutually disinterested agents choose the principles that will govern the basic structure of society. It is the equivalent of drafting a constitution before one knows which caste, class, religion or region one will be born into. Because the choosers are free and equal and the procedure is fair, whatever principles emerge are by definition just: this is the sense in which fairness generates justice.

deprives each chooser of knowledge of his class, caste, race, sex, natural talents and conception of the good — he knows only that he could turn out to be anyone. Not knowing whether he will be a Delhi industrialist or a landless Dalit, he becomes risk-averse and applies the
rule: choose the alternative whose worst possible outcome is the best among the worst outcomes. The society so designed is one you would accept even if ‘your enemy were to assign you your place’.
The chosen principles govern the distribution of
— liberty, rights, opportunity, income, wealth and the social bases of self-respect, which any rational person wants whatever else he wants. First, each person has an
equal right to the most extensive basic liberty
compatible with a like liberty for all. Second, social and economic inequalities must be attached to positions open under
greatest benefit of the least advantaged
: the first must be fully met before the second is entertained, so no measure of poverty relief may be traded against the right to vote or to free speech.

permits inequality only where it improves the position of the worst-off — a surgeon may earn many times a clerk if that differential is what staffs rural health centres, and reservation is defended on exactly this logic. Since the natural distribution of talents is ‘neither just nor unjust’ — what matters is how institutions respond to it — Rawls ‘democratises’ equality, and the advantaged accept the arrangement as rational social insurance taken out behind the veil. It is thus ‘the best possible utilisation of inequality’, distinct from socialism’s ‘equal poverty’.
in form — a hypothetical agreement reviving Locke, Rousseau and Kant — and

in substance, since its second principle redistributes primary goods to secure the least advantaged. Wedding liberty to social equality is precisely how Rawls enriched liberalism, converting it from a doctrine of non-interference into one of positive obligation. As
conceded, political philosophers must now “either work within Rawls’ theory or explain why not.”
Q — Make a comparative assessment of the Greek (Plato and Aristotle) perspective of justice with the Rawlsian concept of justice. (UPSC 2020)
Set out the Greek conception, then the Rawlsian, and judge where they diverge and where they quietly converge.
and the basis of a stable order, but fill it with opposite content.
: “each doing his own task, doing it well and doing it only.”
(A varna-like division — rulers rule, soldiers guard, producers produce; injustice is meddling in another’s station.)
(Distributive, corrective and commutative justice — offices go by merit, not by lot.)
— Plato’s ‘myth of the metals’ and Aristotle’s natural slave; women and slaves stand outside the Polis.
: free and equal individuals choose behind the
, so inequality survives only if it lifts the worst-off.
(You cannot defend caste hierarchy if you may yourself be born at its bottom.)

— Greek justice is teleological and community-centred, Rawlsian justice individualist and egalitarian; yet Indian affirmative action echoes both Aristotle’s ‘unequals unequally’ and the difference principle.
Both traditions treat justice as ‘the first virtue of social institutions’ and as the condition of a stable political order, and both make it the organising question of political philosophy —
opens with the same claim. They diverge entirely on content: the Greeks derive justice from an objective natural order, Rawls from a fair procedure of choice among equals.

defines justice as “each element in society doing its appropriate task, doing it well and doing it only” — every person remaining ‘at the station allotted by nature’, so that reason rules through the philosopher-kings, spirit guards through the auxiliaries and appetite produces. The scheme is varna-like: injustice is meddling in another class’s function. Justice is thus a virtue of the soul writ large upon the city, not a rule of distribution among rights-bearing individuals.
: “treating equals equally and unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities.” He divides it into
justice (honours and offices allotted according to merit or desert, not by lot),
justice (the judge restoring what a wrong has disturbed) and
justice (fairness in voluntary exchange). Justice for him is a mean, and ‘complete virtue in relation to another’.
‘myth of the metals’ fixes classes by an alleged natural endowment of gold, silver and bronze;

defends slavery as natural and excludes women, slaves and labourers from citizenship of the Polis. Justice for them conserves an ordered hierarchy of function and desert: each is given his ‘due’, but the due is fixed by nature rather than chosen by the persons concerned.
begins instead from the free and equal individual. Justice is not a pre-given natural order but
— whatever rational choosers would agree upon behind the

, ignorant of their caste, class, sex and talents. Because you might be born at the bottom of the hierarchy, no defence of caste or of natural slavery can survive the test. The outcome is equal basic liberty for all, with inequality permitted only where it works to the greatest benefit of the

The Greek view is teleological and community-centred, justice consisting in fitting into a natural whole; the Rawlsian view is individualist and egalitarian, justice consisting in protecting each person’s inviolable rights. Yet both hold that a stable society must rest on justice, and both allow differential treatment: Indian affirmative action, which treats unequals unequally in order to raise the worst-off, draws simultaneously on
difference principle — proving the two traditions are not wholly opposed.
Q — Examine the communitarian critique of Rawls and assess his response in Political Liberalism. (UPSC 2019)
Two halves — first what the communitarians attack in Rawls, then whether his later political turn answers them.
: the person is not an unencumbered chooser but is
(An Indian is born into a language, caste, faith and family before he ever ‘chooses’ anything — ‘we always wear the glasses of community’.)
— strip away a person’s roles, ties and desires behind the veil and “is anything left of the person?” The Rawlsian self is ‘woefully impoverished’.
: different goods must be distributed by different criteria in separate ‘spheres’.
(Money should buy a car but not a medical seat, a verdict or an election ticket.)
— the ‘atomistic’ individual is a fiction; people ‘flourish only within socially established cooperative activity’, so justice cannot be universal.
(“What is rational in the USA may not be rational in Afghanistan.”)
, not metaphysical, claims and rests stability on an
(Hindu, Muslim and secular Indians endorse the same Constitution for their own different reasons.)
— the critique exposes the thinness of the abstract self, but the political turn lets liberalism live with diversity.
Communitarianism is a reaction against liberalism’s stress on the
— the individual conceived as prior to, and independent of, his ends. Its central claim is that the real person is a

: “we never look at reality with naked eyes; we always wear the glasses of community.” An Indian is born into a language, a caste, a faith and a family long before he chooses anything; the self is therefore not prior to its ends but
Liberalism and the Limits of Justice

, attacks Rawls’ ‘conception of the self’ rather than his principles. If the veil of ignorance strips a person of his desires, roles, attachments and conception of the good, “is anything left of the person?” The chooser in the original position is ‘woefully impoverished’ — a ghost with preferences but no identity — and principles chosen by such a phantom cannot bind real, historically located people.
, denies that one formula can govern all goods: “different goods ought to be distributed differently, for different reasons, by different agents.” His

holds that each social good has its own sphere with its own criterion — money may rightly buy a car but must not buy a medical seat, a judicial verdict or an election ticket. Injustice is ‘dominance’, the invasion of one sphere by the currency of another; hence justice is ‘not the science of homogenisation but the art of differentiation’.
faults Rawls’ ‘atomistic’ individual, insisting that the individual’s well-being presupposes the good of the community which makes autonomy possible in the first place;

, holds that people ‘flourish only within socially established cooperative activity’ and that moral reasoning is intelligible only inside a tradition. The shared conclusion is that there is no universal justice — “what is rational in the USA may not be rational in Afghanistan.”
Rawls accommodates the critique without surrendering his principles. He
limits their scope to the basic political institutions
, offering a ‘political, not metaphysical’ conception of justice that takes no position on the good life and therefore presupposes no thin metaphysical self. Stability is then grounded in an

: citizens holding rival comprehensive doctrines — Hindu, Muslim, Christian, secular-liberal — can endorse the same political principles for their own distinct reasons, which makes the agreement moral and durable rather than a merely prudential Hobbesian
. It rests on public reason, reciprocity and the ‘burdens of judgement’ that make reasonable disagreement permanent.

The communitarians rightly expose the thinness of the abstract self and the plurality of social goods, and their influence is visible in multiculturalism and in Indian debates on personal law and group rights. But Rawls’ political turn shows that liberalism can coexist with cultural diversity: justice as fairness survives as the shared political framework of a plural society, even if it can no longer claim to be a universal metaphysics.
Q — Critically examine Nozick’s libertarian entitlement theory of justice as a critique of Rawls.
Explain how Nozick shifts justice from the pattern of holdings to their history, and then weigh the cost of that shift.
you got what you hold, not the shape of the final distribution.
(A lopsided income chart is not unjust in itself if every rupee arrived by fair means.)
of past wrongs; pass all three and the title is absolute.
(Tendulkar is rich because millions freely bought tickets — perfectly just.)
— “progressive taxation is like bonded labour”; echoing
, ‘social justice is a mirage’, since only persons and not outcomes can be just.
— a ‘night-watchman’ confined to protection and contract enforcement, with the
exception where a life-threatening monopoly justifies intervention.
— it ‘makes the welfare of the poor depend on the justice of the rich’ and ignores that holdings owe as much to chance as to talent.
(Nothing in it corrects inherited caste disability or landlessness.)
— a powerful foil to Rawls rather than a self-standing theory of justice.

: a distribution is just if it arose through a sequence of just steps, whatever shape it finally takes, so a lopsided income chart is not unjust in itself. Any patterned principle — to each according to need, merit or the difference principle — must be continuously enforced against people’s voluntary choices; hence Rawls “compromises liberty for the sake of equality” and violates human dignity.
— original appropriation from nature is legitimate so long as no one else is made worse off; (2)
— voluntary exchange and gift, which treat the other as an end and never merely as a means, a Kantian premise Nozick shares with Rawls; and (3)
— correction of holdings tainted by past theft or conquest. If a holding survives all three tests the owner has an absolute right to it.
wealth, arising because millions freely paid to watch him bat, is the model case of a just holding.
It follows that the state may not take from A to give to B: “progressive taxation is like bonded labour,” since taxing earnings appropriates hours of a person’s life without consent. Echoing
— only human actions, not impersonal market outcomes, can be called just or unjust, and no one designed the distribution that redistribution proposes to correct.
The only justifiable state is the

, limited to the protection of person and property, the enforcement of contracts and defence, with ‘no role in distributive justice’; anything more extensive violates rights. His single concession is the
case: where one person’s monopoly over the only source of water threatens life itself, intervention becomes permissible — an admission that even libertarian rights bend before survival.

The theory ‘makes the welfare of the poor dependent on the justice of the rich’, reducing relief to charity, and in practice defends existing oppression in the name of justice. It ignores that ‘what a person possesses is not due to talent alone’ but to accidents of birth, inheritance and social structure — nothing in the three principles corrects inherited caste disability or landlessness, and rectification is practically unworkable across centuries. The text itself judges it “just a criticism of Rawls from a libertarian point of view — not a sound theory in comparison to Rawls.”

Nozick powerfully defends liberty, property and the separateness of persons against Rawlsian redistribution, and forces liberalism to justify every coercive transfer. But by reducing the state to a guardian of holdings he leaves the disadvantaged at the mercy of the market, which is why his theory is read as an indispensable foil to Rawls rather than as a self-standing account of justice.
Q — Analyse Amartya Sen’s methodological critique of Rawls — social choice vs rational choice, Niti vs Nyaya, and the realization/capability approach.
Show that Sen attacks Rawls’ method rather than his goal, and set out what he puts in its place.
, not about ends: Sen shares the egalitarian goal but denies that justice can be deduced from an imaginary bargain.
— ‘real persons negotiating in real-life situations’ replace ‘abstract individuals in abstract situations’.
(Ask actual Indian citizens about MGNREGA, not phantoms behind a veil.)
is justice as it actually turns out in people’s lives.
(A flawless Right to Education Act is Niti; children actually learning to read is Nyaya.)
: Carla (can play it), Bob (has no other toy), Ann (made it) — utilitarian, egalitarian and libertarian claims, all reasonable, none absolute.
— justice means expanding real freedoms, ‘development as freedom’, and removing manifest injustice.
(Not the size of the transfer but whether a girl can actually reach school and read.)
— Sen reorients Rawls from ideal institutions to real lives, making justice comparative rather than transcendental.

rather than substantive: he accepts Rawls’ egalitarian purpose and calls him the outstanding political philosopher of the age, but denies that a workable theory of justice can be deduced from a hypothetical bargain among idealised agents. Rawls answers ‘what would perfectly just institutions look like?’; Sen holds that the urgent question is ‘how do we make this society less unjust than it is?’
framework — ‘abstract individuals negotiating in abstract situations’ — in favour of the

tradition of Condorcet and Arrow: ‘real persons negotiating in real-life situations’, reasoning publicly and comparing feasible alternatives. Judgments on MGNREGA or on reservation must issue from actual public reasoning among affected citizens, not from phantoms behind a veil; and Sen adds the
borrowed from Adam Smith to correct parochial bias without pretending to unanimity.
denotes organisational propriety and behavioural correctness — the perfect rulebook, which is where Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’ belongs, being procedural, institutional and
denotes justice as it is actually

in the lives people are able to lead. A flawless Right to Education Act is Niti; whether children in a Bihar village can actually read is Nyaya. Since ‘substance is more important than procedure’, Sen’s approach is
where Rawls’ is deontological — matsyanyaya, the ‘justice of the fish’ in which the big devour the small, must be prevented in fact and not merely prohibited on paper.
Against Rawls’ claim that one unique set of principles would be chosen, Sen offers the parable of the

: Carla claims it because she alone can play it (the utilitarian or best-use claim), Bob because he is poorest and has no other toy (the egalitarian claim), and Ann because she made it with her own hands (the libertarian claim). All three arguments are reasonable and none is decisive, so plural competing principles must be reconciled through public reasoning. In the
debate of the Gita he likewise finds Arjuna’s consequentialist anxiety — that countless lives would be destroyed — as compelling as Krishna’s deontological insistence on duty.
: what matters is not the bundle of primary goods a person holds but the

— the real freedoms — he has to be and to do what he has reason to value, since equal income buys very unequal functioning for a disabled or a socially excluded person. Justice means expanding these freedoms, ‘development as freedom’, and removing manifest injustice; the test is not the size of the transfer but whether a girl can actually reach school, read and choose. This reasoning underpins the Human Development Index.

Sen does not overthrow Rawls so much as reorient him — from ideal institutions to real lives, from arrangement to realisation, from the transcendental to the comparative. His critique makes justice practical and actionable, better suited to a diverse world in which perfectly just institutions may never be agreed upon but manifest injustices can still be identified and removed.
Q — Discuss the types and dimensions of justice — distributive (David Miller), procedural vs substantive, retributive, and social/political/economic/legal. (UPSC 2018)
Classify the forms justice takes and show how each answers a different question about sharing, procedure or punishment.
— the fair sharing of resources and opportunities, the defining concern of the welfare state.
(Who gets the college seat, the subsidised grain, the reserved post?)
(solidarity community, Kropotkin) — need being ‘the most appropriate’.
— fair rules versus a fair outcome.
(‘Procedure established by law’ vs ‘due process’ — Maneka Gandhi moved Article 21 from the first to the second.)
— punishment proportioned to the crime (Aristotle, Kant, Hegel), criticised for ignoring the offender, yielding to reform and reconciliation.
— equal access regardless of birth; power-sharing (suffrage, reservation); a dignified livelihood; and enforcement of law, which ‘may or may not’ be morally just.
(Untouchability and apartheid were legal but unjust.)
— the dimensions interlock; the modern welfare state, guided by Rawls and Sen, tilts from procedure toward substantive, need-based justice.
Justice takes different forms depending on what is being distributed, corrected or enforced.

concerns the fair allocation of resources, offices and opportunities — who gets the college seat, the subsidised grain, the reserved post — and is the defining concern of the modern welfare state. Schools differ sharply on its scope: classical liberals want minimal intervention,
, argues that each criterion of distribution belongs to a type of society: distribution by
suits a hierarchical order and is associated with
suits a competitive market society and
. Miller holds the last to be ‘the most appropriate’, which aligns social justice with welfare provision rather than with mere reward for merit.

operates ‘at the level of application’ — the letter of the law, equality before law, ‘procedure established by law’ — and inspires the minimal state, since it demands only that the rules be applied impartially.
— the spirit of the law, ‘due process’ — and encourages state intervention. The Indian illustration is decisive: in
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
the Supreme Court read Article 21 as requiring a procedure that is ‘just, fair and reasonable’, shifting Indian constitutional law from procedural to substantive justice.

, fixes punishment in proportion to the crime and treats the penalty as the criminal’s own desert rather than as a mere instrument of deterrence. It is criticised for attending only to the act while ignoring the offender’s circumstances and the victim’s healing, and so gives way to
, which aim at reform, reparation and reconciliation — the logic of juvenile justice boards, plea bargaining and truth commissions.
means equal access to goods and opportunities irrespective of the circumstances of birth — caste, sex, religion or region.
concerns the sharing of power: universal suffrage, free elections and reservation of seats.
demands equal opportunity to earn a dignified livelihood and freedom from exploitation.

is the impartial enforcement of established law, which ‘may or may not’ be morally just — untouchability in India and apartheid in South Africa were perfectly legal and wholly unjust — which is why legal justice must always be tested against social justice.

These dimensions interlock rather than compete: legal and political justice supply the framework within which claims can be pressed, while distributive and substantive justice supply the content of those claims. The Indian Preamble’s pledge of ‘justice — social, economic and political’ captures the combination, and the modern welfare state, guided by
, tilts the balance decisively from mere procedure toward substantive, need-based justice.
Q — “Justice is an architectonic and dynamic idea.” Discuss its importance in political philosophy and how conceptions of justice have evolved.
Unpack the two adjectives — why justice is foundational, and why its content keeps moving.
(to bind): justice binds people into a fair order by giving each his due.
— the master value that organises every other concept: liberty, equality and rights are all argued out as questions of justice.
— people obey institutions “only when they find them just”, so justice underwrites legitimacy and stability.
(From Champaran to today’s protest movements, resistance is framed as injustice, not illegality.)
— the ideal is fixed but our grasp of it is ‘a continuous process’ tracking social consciousness (
(Slavery, untouchability and the subordination of women were once ‘just’; all are now condemned.)

— Plato (natural station) → Aristotle (proportion) → Hobbes (the sovereign’s command) → utilitarians (hedonistic calculus) → Marx (ending class exploitation) → today ‘redistribution based on affirmative action’.
— architectonic as the foundation of legitimate order, dynamic as a moving frontier of moral progress.
(to bind), justice ‘binds people into a fair order of relationships by giving each their due’. Its classic formulation is
— to each his own — but the content of that ‘own’ is precisely what every theory disputes.
states its standing definitively: “justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought.”
around which the whole of Western political philosophy is organised: liberty, equality, rights, property and punishment are ultimately argued out as questions about what is just.
makes it ‘complete virtue in relation to another’. It is architectonic in the builder’s sense — the design principle that determines how all the other values are fitted together.

Its centrality is practical and not merely academic: people accept and obey institutions “only when they find them just”, so justice underpins political obligation, legitimacy and stability itself. Resistance is characteristically framed as a charge of injustice rather than of illegality — from Champaran and the Salt Satyagraha to contemporary farm and anti-corruption agitations — which is why an unjust order must rest on coercion where a just one rests on consent.
Although justice embodies an ideal ‘akin to absolute truth’, our apprehension of it is ‘a continuous process’ that tracks changing

calls this ‘modern consciousness’: slavery and serfdom were once held just in Europe, untouchability in India, and the subordination of women almost everywhere — all are now condemned. A defensible conception of justice must therefore rest on
read in the light of the prevailing social consciousness, which makes justice a moving rather than a settled standard.
(each at the station allotted by nature) and
(justice is obedience to the sovereign’s command, there being no justice in the state of nature) and the
(the hedonistic calculus of the greatest happiness), to the
(justice as the abolition of class exploitation) and, in our own time, to ‘redistribution based on affirmative action’ as elaborated by

As an architectonic idea justice is the foundation of legitimate political order, the value from which all the others take their bearings; as a dynamic idea it is a moving frontier of moral progress that each generation must redraw. That is why every major work of political philosophy, from Plato to Rawls and Sen, turns out on inspection to be a theory of justice.
: ‘justice is the first virtue of social institutions’; justice = fairness; deontological (Kantian).
→ choose fair principles not knowing your place.
(1) equal basic liberty; (2) fair equality of opportunity + difference principle (help the least advantaged) — in lexical order.
: justice = each doing his own duty (station by nature);
: entitlement theory (acquisition/transfer/rectification); ‘tax = forced labour’; minimal state.
: social choice > rational choice; Niti vs Nyaya (realization-focused); three children & a flute; capability approach.
(Sandel, Walzer, Taylor, MacIntyre): the ‘situated self’; ‘justice is the art of differentiation, not homogenisation’.
Liberalism and the Limits of Justice
: political (not metaphysical) conception; overlapping consensus (vs modus vivendi).
: 3 principles of distributive justice — rights (Hume), desert (Spencer), need (Kropotkin).
: Rawls does NOT extend the difference principle between societies; ‘decent peoples’.
original position + veil of ignorance + maximin → 2 principles (equal liberty; fair opportunity + difference principle) in lexical order; contractual + distributive; democratic equality.
Plato (station by nature) & Aristotle (proportional) justify hierarchy; Rawls builds egalitarian, individual-rights justice.
Sandel/Walzer/Taylor/MacIntyre — situated self, complex equality; Rawls’ reply = political conception + overlapping consensus.
entitlement theory (acquisition/transfer/rectification); minimal state; tax = forced labour; welfare of poor left to the rich.
social choice > rational choice; Niti vs Nyaya; capability / ‘development as freedom’; three children & a flute.
distributive (Miller: rights/desert/need), procedural vs substantive (Maneka Gandhi), retributive; social/political/economic/legal.
first virtue of institutions; evolves with social consciousness (Raphael); Plato→utilitarians→Marx→affirmative action.

Rawls — ‘each person possesses an inviolability founded on justice’; Sandel — ‘is anything left of the person?’; Walzer — ‘different goods distributed differently’; Hayek — ‘social justice is a mirage’.

(UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 3) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  justice as an architectonic and dynamic idea; classical (Plato, Aristotle) and modern theories; the types/dimensions of justice (distributive, procedural vs substantive, retributive); Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’; and its critiques — Nozick (libertarian), Amartya Sen (methodological) and the communitarians (Sandel, Walzer, Taylor, MacIntyre), with Rawls’ reply in Political Liberalism. Must-know thinkers:  Plato, Aristotle, Hume, David Miller, John Rawls, Robert Nozick, Amartya Sen, Ronald Dworkin, Michael Sandel, Michael Walzer, Charles Taylor, Alasdair MacIntyre, Carole Gilligan, Thomas Pogge, A.V. Dicey. PYQ trend:  Rawls dominates — original position (2013), difference principle (2015), contractual & distributive (2017), justification of discrimination (2018), Rawls enriching liberalism (2021); plus Greek vs Rawlsian (2020), communitarian perspectives (2019) and distributive justice (2018). Master Questions Q — Explain Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’ — the original position, veil of ignorance, primary goods, maximin, the two principles and lexical order, the difference principle and democratic equality. Is it both contractual and distributive? (UPSC 2013/2015/2017/2018/2021) What it’s asking:  Lay out Rawls’ machinery step by step, then prove it is at once a social contract and a scheme of redistribution. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Premise  — anti-utilitarian, Kantian,  deontological : no person may be sacrificed for the aggregate.  (Utilitarianism could justify displacing a tribal village for a dam because more people gain; Rawls forbids it.) 2. Original position  — a hypothetical ‘thought experiment’ in which rational, mutually disinterested people frame the rules before society exists.  (Like drafting the Constitution before knowing which caste, class or religion you will be born into.) 3. Veil of ignorance + maximin  — stripped of knowledge of class, caste, sex and talent, risk-averse agents pick the option whose  worst  outcome is best.  (Not knowing whether you will be born a Delhi industrialist or a landless Dalit, you insure the bottom rung.) 4. Two principles in lexical order  — (1) equal basic liberty; (2) fair equality of opportunity + the difference principle.  Lexical order  = principle 1 must be fully satisfied before 2 is even considered.  (No amount of poverty relief may buy away the right to vote or to free speech.) 5. Difference principle & democratic equality  — inequality is legitimate only if it lifts the  worst-off .  (A surgeon may earn ten times a clerk if the higher pay is what staffs rural PHCs; reservation is defended on the same logic.) 6. Contractual and distributive  — a hypothetical agreement (Locke, Rousseau, Kant) that also redistributes  primary goods ; this is how Rawls ‘enriched’ liberalism. Model Answer 1. Premise.  John Rawls , whom the text calls “the greatest political philosopher of the 20th century,” revived normative theory in  A Theory of Justice (1971)  with ‘justice as fairness’. He writes against  utilitarianism , which permits the individual to be sacrificed for the ‘greatest happiness of the greatest number’ — as when a tribal village is displaced for a dam because the aggregate gain is larger. Reviving the  Kantian  tradition of human dignity, his theory is  deontological : “each person possesses an inviolability founded on justice that even the welfare of society as a whole cannot override.” 2. Original position.  The  original position  is a hypothetical, purely procedural ‘thought experiment’ — not a historical state of nature — in which rational, mutually disinterested agents choose the principles that will govern the basic structure of society. It is the equivalent of drafting a constitution before one knows which caste, class, religion or region one will be born into. Because the choosers are free and equal and the procedure is fair, whatever principles emerge are by definition just: this is the sense in which fairness generates justice. 3. Veil of ignorance and maximin.  Within the original position the  veil of ignorance  deprives each chooser of knowledge of his class, caste, race, sex, natural talents and conception of the good — he knows only that he could turn out to be anyone. Not knowing whether he will be a Delhi industrialist or a landless Dalit, he becomes risk-averse and applies the  maximin  rule: choose the alternative whose worst possible outcome is the best among the worst outcomes. The society so designed is one you would accept even if ‘your enemy were to assign you your place’. 4. Two principles in lexical order.  The chosen principles govern the distribution of  primary goods  — liberty, rights, opportunity, income, wealth and the social bases of self-respect, which any rational person wants whatever else he wants. First, each person has an  equal right to the most extensive basic liberty  compatible with a like liberty for all. Second, social and economic inequalities must be attached to positions open under  fair equality of opportunity  and arranged to the  greatest benefit of the least advantaged . They hold in  lexical (serial) order : the first must be fully met before the second is entertained, so no measure of poverty relief may be traded against the right to vote or to free speech. 5. Difference principle and democratic equality.  The  difference principle  permits inequality only where it improves the position of the worst-off — a surgeon may earn many times a clerk if that differential is what staffs rural health centres, and reservation is defended on exactly this logic. Since the natural distribution of talents is ‘neither just nor unjust’ — what matters is how institutions respond to it — Rawls ‘democratises’ equality, and the advantaged accept the arrangement as rational social insurance taken out behind the veil. It is thus ‘the best possible utilisation of inequality’, distinct from socialism’s ‘equal poverty’. 6. Contractual and distributive.  The theory is  contractual  in form — a hypothetical agreement reviving Locke, Rousseau and Kant — and  distributive  in substance, since its second principle redistributes primary goods to secure the least advantaged. Wedding liberty to social equality is precisely how Rawls enriched liberalism, converting it from a doctrine of non-interference into one of positive obligation. As  Nozick  conceded, political philosophers must now “either work within Rawls’ theory or explain why not.” Q — Make a comparative assessment of the Greek (Plato and Aristotle) perspective of justice with the Rawlsian concept of justice. (UPSC 2020) What it’s asking:  Set out the Greek conception, then the Rawlsian, and judge where they diverge and where they quietly converge. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Common ground  — both make justice the  first virtue of social institutions  and the basis of a stable order, but fill it with opposite content. 2. Plato — functional harmony : “each doing his own task, doing it well and doing it only.”  (A varna-like division — rulers rule, soldiers guard, producers produce; injustice is meddling in another’s station.) 3. Aristotle — proportional justice : “treat equals equally and unequals unequally.”  (Distributive, corrective and commutative justice — offices go by merit, not by lot.) 4. Both accept natural inequality  — Plato’s ‘myth of the metals’ and Aristotle’s natural slave; women and slaves stand outside the Polis. 5. Rawls — fairness, not station : free and equal individuals choose behind the  veil of ignorance , so inequality survives only if it lifts the worst-off.  (You cannot defend caste hierarchy if you may yourself be born at its bottom.) 6. Assessment  — Greek justice is teleological and community-centred, Rawlsian justice individualist and egalitarian; yet Indian affirmative action echoes both Aristotle’s ‘unequals unequally’ and the difference principle. Model Answer 1. Common ground.  Both traditions treat justice as ‘the first virtue of social institutions’ and as the condition of a stable political order, and both make it the organising question of political philosophy —  The Republic  is subtitled ‘concerning justice’ and  A Theory of Justice  opens with the same claim. They diverge entirely on content: the Greeks derive justice from an objective natural order, Rawls from a fair procedure of choice among equals. 2. Plato — functional harmony.  Plato  in  The Republic  defines justice as “each element in society doing its appropriate task, doing it well and doing it only” — every person remaining ‘at the station allotted by nature’, so that reason rules through the philosopher-kings, spirit guards through the auxiliaries and appetite produces. The scheme is varna-like: injustice is meddling in another class’s function. Justice is thus a virtue of the soul writ large upon the city, not a rule of distribution among rights-bearing individuals. 3. Aristotle — proportional justice.  Aristotle  makes justice  proportional : “treating equals equally and unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities.” He divides it into  distributive  justice (honours and offices allotted according to merit or desert, not by lot),  corrective  justice (the judge restoring what a wrong has disturbed) and  commutative  justice (fairness in voluntary exchange). Justice for him is a mean, and ‘complete virtue in relation to another’. 4. Both accept natural inequality.  Neither Greek is an egalitarian.  Plato’s  ‘myth of the metals’ fixes classes by an alleged natural endowment of gold, silver and bronze;  Aristotle  defends slavery as natural and excludes women, slaves and labourers from citizenship of the Polis. Justice for them conserves an ordered hierarchy of function and desert: each is given his ‘due’, but the due is fixed by nature rather than chosen by the persons concerned. 5. Rawls — fairness, not station.  Rawls  begins instead from the free and equal individual. Justice is not a pre-given natural order but  fairness  — whatever rational choosers would agree upon behind the  veil of ignorance , ignorant of their caste, class, sex and talents. Because you might be born at the bottom of the hierarchy, no defence of caste or of natural slavery can survive the test. The outcome is equal basic liberty for all, with inequality permitted only where it works to the greatest benefit of the  least advantaged . 6. Assessment.  The Greek view is teleological and community-centred, justice consisting in fitting into a natural whole; the Rawlsian view is individualist and egalitarian, justice consisting in protecting each person’s inviolable rights. Yet both hold that a stable society must rest on justice, and both allow differential treatment: Indian affirmative action, which treats unequals unequally in order to raise the worst-off, draws simultaneously on  Aristotle’s  proportional justice and  Rawls’  difference principle — proving the two traditions are not wholly opposed. Q — Examine the communitarian critique of Rawls and assess his response in Political Liberalism. (UPSC 2019) What it’s asking:  Two halves — first what the communitarians attack in Rawls, then whether his later political turn answers them. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core claim — the situated self : the person is not an unencumbered chooser but is  constituted  by community.  (An Indian is born into a language, caste, faith and family before he ever ‘chooses’ anything — ‘we always wear the glasses of community’.) 2. Sandel  — strip away a person’s roles, ties and desires behind the veil and “is anything left of the person?” The Rawlsian self is ‘woefully impoverished’. 3. Walzer — complex equality : different goods must be distributed by different criteria in separate ‘spheres’.  (Money should buy a car but not a medical seat, a verdict or an election ticket.) 4. Taylor & MacIntyre  — the ‘atomistic’ individual is a fiction; people ‘flourish only within socially established cooperative activity’, so justice cannot be universal.  (“What is rational in the USA may not be rational in Afghanistan.”) 5. Rawls’ reply  — in  Political Liberalism  he narrows the theory to  political , not metaphysical, claims and rests stability on an  overlapping consensus .  (Hindu, Muslim and secular Indians endorse the same Constitution for their own different reasons.) 6. Conclusion  — the critique exposes the thinness of the abstract self, but the political turn lets liberalism live with diversity. Model Answer 1. Core claim — the situated self.  Communitarianism is a reaction against liberalism’s stress on the  autonomous, unencumbered self  — the individual conceived as prior to, and independent of, his ends. Its central claim is that the real person is a  ‘situated (embedded) self’ : “we never look at reality with naked eyes; we always wear the glasses of community.” An Indian is born into a language, a caste, a faith and a family long before he chooses anything; the self is therefore not prior to its ends but  constituted by them . 2. Sandel.  Michael Sandel , in  Liberalism and the Limits of Justice , attacks Rawls’ ‘conception of the self’ rather than his principles. If the veil of ignorance strips a person of his desires, roles, attachments and conception of the good, “is anything left of the person?” The chooser in the original position is ‘woefully impoverished’ — a ghost with preferences but no identity — and principles chosen by such a phantom cannot bind real, historically located people. 3. Walzer — complex equality.  Michael Walzer , in  Spheres of Justice , denies that one formula can govern all goods: “different goods ought to be distributed differently, for different reasons, by different agents.” His  complex equality  holds that each social good has its own sphere with its own criterion — money may rightly buy a car but must not buy a medical seat, a judicial verdict or an election ticket. Injustice is ‘dominance’, the invasion of one sphere by the currency of another; hence justice is ‘not the science of homogenisation but the art of differentiation’. 4. Taylor and MacIntyre.  Charles Taylor  faults Rawls’ ‘atomistic’ individual, insisting that the individual’s well-being presupposes the good of the community which makes autonomy possible in the first place;  Alasdair MacIntyre , in  After Virtue , holds that people ‘flourish only within socially established cooperative activity’ and that moral reasoning is intelligible only inside a tradition. The shared conclusion is that there is no universal justice — “what is rational in the USA may not be rational in Afghanistan.” 5. Rawls’ reply.  In  Political Liberalism  Rawls accommodates the critique without surrendering his principles. He  limits their scope to the basic political institutions , offering a ‘political, not metaphysical’ conception of justice that takes no position on the good life and therefore presupposes no thin metaphysical self. Stability is then grounded in an  overlapping consensus : citizens holding rival comprehensive doctrines — Hindu, Muslim, Christian, secular-liberal — can endorse the same political principles for their own distinct reasons, which makes the agreement moral and durable rather than a merely prudential Hobbesian  modus vivendi . It rests on public reason, reciprocity and the ‘burdens of judgement’ that make reasonable disagreement permanent. 6. Conclusion.  The communitarians rightly expose the thinness of the abstract self and the plurality of social goods, and their influence is visible in multiculturalism and in Indian debates on personal law and group rights. But Rawls’ political turn shows that liberalism can coexist with cultural diversity: justice as fairness survives as the shared political framework of a plural society, even if it can no longer claim to be a universal metaphysics. Q — Critically examine Nozick’s libertarian entitlement theory of justice as a critique of Rawls. What it’s asking:  Explain how Nozick shifts justice from the pattern of holdings to their history, and then weigh the cost of that shift. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Historical, not patterned  — the  entitlement theory  judges  how  you got what you hold, not the shape of the final distribution.  (A lopsided income chart is not unjust in itself if every rupee arrived by fair means.) 2. Three principles  — just  acquisition , just  transfer  and  rectification  of past wrongs; pass all three and the title is absolute.  (Tendulkar is rich because millions freely bought tickets — perfectly just.) 3. Redistribution is illegitimate  — “progressive taxation is like bonded labour”; echoing  Hayek , ‘social justice is a mirage’, since only persons and not outcomes can be just. 4. Minimal state  — a ‘night-watchman’ confined to protection and contract enforcement, with the  single-well  exception where a life-threatening monopoly justifies intervention. 5. Critique  — it ‘makes the welfare of the poor depend on the justice of the rich’ and ignores that holdings owe as much to chance as to talent.  (Nothing in it corrects inherited caste disability or landlessness.) 6. Conclusion  — a powerful foil to Rawls rather than a self-standing theory of justice. Model Answer 1. Historical, not patterned.  Robert Nozick , in  Anarchy, State and Utopia (1974) , answers Rawls with the  entitlement theory . Justice is  historical , not  patterned : a distribution is just if it arose through a sequence of just steps, whatever shape it finally takes, so a lopsided income chart is not unjust in itself. Any patterned principle — to each according to need, merit or the difference principle — must be continuously enforced against people’s voluntary choices; hence Rawls “compromises liberty for the sake of equality” and violates human dignity. 2. Three principles.  Entitlement rests on three rules: (1)  just acquisition  — original appropriation from nature is legitimate so long as no one else is made worse off; (2)  just transfer  — voluntary exchange and gift, which treat the other as an end and never merely as a means, a Kantian premise Nozick shares with Rawls; and (3)  rectification  — correction of holdings tainted by past theft or conquest. If a holding survives all three tests the owner has an absolute right to it.  Sachin Tendulkar’s  wealth, arising because millions freely paid to watch him bat, is the model case of a just holding. 3. Redistribution is illegitimate.  It follows that the state may not take from A to give to B: “progressive taxation is like bonded labour,” since taxing earnings appropriates hours of a person’s life without consent. Echoing  F.A. Hayek , Nozick treats  ‘social justice as a mirage’  — only human actions, not impersonal market outcomes, can be called just or unjust, and no one designed the distribution that redistribution proposes to correct. 4. Minimal state.  The only justifiable state is the  minimal or ‘night-watchman’ state , limited to the protection of person and property, the enforcement of contracts and defence, with ‘no role in distributive justice’; anything more extensive violates rights. His single concession is the  single-well  case: where one person’s monopoly over the only source of water threatens life itself, intervention becomes permissible — an admission that even libertarian rights bend before survival. 5. Critique.  The theory ‘makes the welfare of the poor dependent on the justice of the rich’, reducing relief to charity, and in practice defends existing oppression in the name of justice. It ignores that ‘what a person possesses is not due to talent alone’ but to accidents of birth, inheritance and social structure — nothing in the three principles corrects inherited caste disability or landlessness, and rectification is practically unworkable across centuries. The text itself judges it “just a criticism of Rawls from a libertarian point of view — not a sound theory in comparison to Rawls.” 6. Conclusion.  Nozick powerfully defends liberty, property and the separateness of persons against Rawlsian redistribution, and forces liberalism to justify every coercive transfer. But by reducing the state to a guardian of holdings he leaves the disadvantaged at the mercy of the market, which is why his theory is read as an indispensable foil to Rawls rather than as a self-standing account of justice. Q — Analyse Amartya Sen’s methodological critique of Rawls — social choice vs rational choice, Niti vs Nyaya, and the realization/capability approach. What it’s asking:  Show that Sen attacks Rawls’ method rather than his goal, and set out what he puts in its place. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Nature of the quarrel  —  methodological , not about ends: Sen shares the egalitarian goal but denies that justice can be deduced from an imaginary bargain. 2. Social choice > rational choice  — ‘real persons negotiating in real-life situations’ replace ‘abstract individuals in abstract situations’.  (Ask actual Indian citizens about MGNREGA, not phantoms behind a veil.) 3. Niti vs Nyaya  —  Niti  is the perfect rulebook,  Nyaya  is justice as it actually turns out in people’s lives.  (A flawless Right to Education Act is Niti; children actually learning to read is Nyaya.) 4. No single formula  — the  three children and a flute : Carla (can play it), Bob (has no other toy), Ann (made it) — utilitarian, egalitarian and libertarian claims, all reasonable, none absolute. 5. Capability approach  — justice means expanding real freedoms, ‘development as freedom’, and removing manifest injustice.  (Not the size of the transfer but whether a girl can actually reach school and read.) 6. Conclusion  — Sen reorients Rawls from ideal institutions to real lives, making justice comparative rather than transcendental. Model Answer 1. Nature of the quarrel.  Amartya Sen’s  objection in  The Idea of Justice (2009)  is  methodological  rather than substantive: he accepts Rawls’ egalitarian purpose and calls him the outstanding political philosopher of the age, but denies that a workable theory of justice can be deduced from a hypothetical bargain among idealised agents. Rawls answers ‘what would perfectly just institutions look like?’; Sen holds that the urgent question is ‘how do we make this society less unjust than it is?’ 2. Social choice over rational choice.  Sen rejects Rawls’  rational choice  framework — ‘abstract individuals negotiating in abstract situations’ — in favour of the  social choice  tradition of Condorcet and Arrow: ‘real persons negotiating in real-life situations’, reasoning publicly and comparing feasible alternatives. Judgments on MGNREGA or on reservation must issue from actual public reasoning among affected citizens, not from phantoms behind a veil; and Sen adds the  ‘impartial spectator’  borrowed from Adam Smith to correct parochial bias without pretending to unanimity. 3. Niti versus Nyaya.  Sen recovers two Sanskrit terms.  Niti  denotes organisational propriety and behavioural correctness — the perfect rulebook, which is where Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’ belongs, being procedural, institutional and  transcendental .  Nyaya  denotes justice as it is actually  realised  in the lives people are able to lead. A flawless Right to Education Act is Niti; whether children in a Bihar village can actually read is Nyaya. Since ‘substance is more important than procedure’, Sen’s approach is  consequentialist  where Rawls’ is deontological — matsyanyaya, the ‘justice of the fish’ in which the big devour the small, must be prevented in fact and not merely prohibited on paper. 4. No single formula.  Against Rawls’ claim that one unique set of principles would be chosen, Sen offers the parable of the  three children and a flute : Carla claims it because she alone can play it (the utilitarian or best-use claim), Bob because he is poorest and has no other toy (the egalitarian claim), and Ann because she made it with her own hands (the libertarian claim). All three arguments are reasonable and none is decisive, so plural competing principles must be reconciled through public reasoning. In the  Krishna–Arjuna  debate of the Gita he likewise finds Arjuna’s consequentialist anxiety — that countless lives would be destroyed — as compelling as Krishna’s deontological insistence on duty. 5. Capability approach.  Sen therefore substitutes a  realization-focused capability approach : what matters is not the bundle of primary goods a person holds but the  capabilities  — the real freedoms — he has to be and to do what he has reason to value, since equal income buys very unequal functioning for a disabled or a socially excluded person. Justice means expanding these freedoms, ‘development as freedom’, and removing manifest injustice; the test is not the size of the transfer but whether a girl can actually reach school, read and choose. This reasoning underpins the Human Development Index. 6. Conclusion.  Sen does not overthrow Rawls so much as reorient him — from ideal institutions to real lives, from arrangement to realisation, from the transcendental to the comparative. His critique makes justice practical and actionable, better suited to a diverse world in which perfectly just institutions may never be agreed upon but manifest injustices can still be identified and removed. Q — Discuss the types and dimensions of justice — distributive (David Miller), procedural vs substantive, retributive, and social/political/economic/legal. (UPSC 2018) What it’s asking:  Classify the forms justice takes and show how each answers a different question about sharing, procedure or punishment. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Distributive justice  — the fair sharing of resources and opportunities, the defining concern of the welfare state.  (Who gets the college seat, the subsidised grain, the reserved post?) 2. Miller’s three principles  — distribution by  rights  (hierarchical order, Hume), by  desert  (competitive market, Spencer) and by  need  (solidarity community, Kropotkin) — need being ‘the most appropriate’. 3. Procedural vs substantive  — fair rules versus a fair outcome.  (‘Procedure established by law’ vs ‘due process’ — Maneka Gandhi moved Article 21 from the first to the second.) 4. Retributive → restorative  — punishment proportioned to the crime (Aristotle, Kant, Hegel), criticised for ignoring the offender, yielding to reform and reconciliation.  (Juvenile boards and plea bargaining.) 5. Social / political / economic / legal  — equal access regardless of birth; power-sharing (suffrage, reservation); a dignified livelihood; and enforcement of law, which ‘may or may not’ be morally just.  (Untouchability and apartheid were legal but unjust.) 6. Conclusion  — the dimensions interlock; the modern welfare state, guided by Rawls and Sen, tilts from procedure toward substantive, need-based justice. Model Answer 1. Distributive justice.  Justice takes different forms depending on what is being distributed, corrected or enforced.  Distributive justice  concerns the fair allocation of resources, offices and opportunities — who gets the college seat, the subsidised grain, the reserved post — and is the defining concern of the modern welfare state. Schools differ sharply on its scope: classical liberals want minimal intervention,  Nozick  almost none,  Rawls  the difference principle, and  Sen  the building of capabilities. 2. Miller’s three principles.  David Miller , in  Social Justice , argues that each criterion of distribution belongs to a type of society: distribution by  rights  suits a hierarchical order and is associated with  Hume ; by  desert  suits a competitive market society and  Spencer ; and by  need  suits a solidarity community and  Kropotkin . Miller holds the last to be ‘the most appropriate’, which aligns social justice with welfare provision rather than with mere reward for merit. 3. Procedural versus substantive.  Procedural justice  operates ‘at the level of application’ — the letter of the law, equality before law, ‘procedure established by law’ — and inspires the minimal state, since it demands only that the rules be applied impartially.  Substantive justice  looks to the  outcome  — the spirit of the law, ‘due process’ — and encourages state intervention. The Indian illustration is decisive: in  Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)  the Supreme Court read Article 21 as requiring a procedure that is ‘just, fair and reasonable’, shifting Indian constitutional law from procedural to substantive justice. 4. Retributive to restorative.  Retributive justice , rooted in  Aristotle ,  Kant  and  Hegel , fixes punishment in proportion to the crime and treats the penalty as the criminal’s own desert rather than as a mere instrument of deterrence. It is criticised for attending only to the act while ignoring the offender’s circumstances and the victim’s healing, and so gives way to  restorative and transformative justice , which aim at reform, reparation and reconciliation — the logic of juvenile justice boards, plea bargaining and truth commissions. 5. Social, political, economic and legal.  Social justice  means equal access to goods and opportunities irrespective of the circumstances of birth — caste, sex, religion or region.  Political justice  concerns the sharing of power: universal suffrage, free elections and reservation of seats.  Economic justice  demands equal opportunity to earn a dignified livelihood and freedom from exploitation.  Legal justice  is the impartial enforcement of established law, which ‘may or may not’ be morally just — untouchability in India and apartheid in South Africa were perfectly legal and wholly unjust — which is why legal justice must always be tested against social justice. 6. Conclusion.  These dimensions interlock rather than compete: legal and political justice supply the framework within which claims can be pressed, while distributive and substantive justice supply the content of those claims. The Indian Preamble’s pledge of ‘justice — social, economic and political’ captures the combination, and the modern welfare state, guided by  Rawls  and  Sen , tilts the balance decisively from mere procedure toward substantive, need-based justice. Q — “Justice is an architectonic and dynamic idea.” Discuss its importance in political philosophy and how conceptions of justice have evolved. What it’s asking:  Unpack the two adjectives — why justice is foundational, and why its content keeps moving. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Meaning  — from the Latin  jus  (a bond) and  jungere  (to bind): justice binds people into a fair order by giving each his due.  Rawls : ‘the first virtue of social institutions’. 2. Architectonic  — the master value that organises every other concept: liberty, equality and rights are all argued out as questions of justice.  ( The Republic  is subtitled ‘concerning justice’.) 3. Basis of obligation  — people obey institutions “only when they find them just”, so justice underwrites legitimacy and stability.  (From Champaran to today’s protest movements, resistance is framed as injustice, not illegality.) 4. Dynamic  — the ideal is fixed but our grasp of it is ‘a continuous process’ tracking social consciousness ( D.D. Raphael ).  (Slavery, untouchability and the subordination of women were once ‘just’; all are now condemned.) 5. Evolution  — Plato (natural station) → Aristotle (proportion) → Hobbes (the sovereign’s command) → utilitarians (hedonistic calculus) → Marx (ending class exploitation) → today ‘redistribution based on affirmative action’. 6. Conclusion  — architectonic as the foundation of legitimate order, dynamic as a moving frontier of moral progress. Model Answer 1. Meaning.  Derived from the Latin  jus  (a bond) and  jungere  (to bind), justice ‘binds people into a fair order of relationships by giving each their due’. Its classic formulation is  suum cuique  — to each his own — but the content of that ‘own’ is precisely what every theory disputes.  Rawls  states its standing definitively: “justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought.” 2. Architectonic.  Justice is the  master or foundational value  around which the whole of Western political philosophy is organised: liberty, equality, rights, property and punishment are ultimately argued out as questions about what is just.  Plato’s   Republic  is subtitled ‘concerning justice’, and  Aristotle  makes it ‘complete virtue in relation to another’. It is architectonic in the builder’s sense — the design principle that determines how all the other values are fitted together. 3. Basis of obligation.  Its centrality is practical and not merely academic: people accept and obey institutions “only when they find them just”, so justice underpins political obligation, legitimacy and stability itself. Resistance is characteristically framed as a charge of injustice rather than of illegality — from Champaran and the Salt Satyagraha to contemporary farm and anti-corruption agitations — which is why an unjust order must rest on coercion where a just one rests on consent. 4. Dynamic.  Although justice embodies an ideal ‘akin to absolute truth’, our apprehension of it is ‘a continuous process’ that tracks changing  social consciousness .  D.D. Raphael  calls this ‘modern consciousness’: slavery and serfdom were once held just in Europe, untouchability in India, and the subordination of women almost everywhere — all are now condemned. A defensible conception of justice must therefore rest on  reason  read in the light of the prevailing social consciousness, which makes justice a moving rather than a settled standard. 5. Evolution.  Conceptions have accordingly shifted: from  Plato  (each at the station allotted by nature) and  Aristotle  (proportional equality), through  Hobbes  (justice is obedience to the sovereign’s command, there being no justice in the state of nature) and the  utilitarians  (the hedonistic calculus of the greatest happiness), to the  Marxists  (justice as the abolition of class exploitation) and, in our own time, to ‘redistribution based on affirmative action’ as elaborated by  Rawls  and  Sen . 6. Conclusion.  As an architectonic idea justice is the foundation of legitimate political order, the value from which all the others take their bearings; as a dynamic idea it is a moving frontier of moral progress that each generation must redraw. That is why every major work of political philosophy, from Plato to Rawls and Sen, turns out on inspection to be a theory of justice.
